title: Lesson 5: Tokens, Context Windows, and Cost Engineering for Agent Workloads
description: Agents don't just use tokens; they burn them: roughly 4x a chat conversation, 15x for multi-agent. The four levers that control the bill (budgeting, compression, caching, and model routing), with the math worked out on a real 10-agent pipeline.

questions.question: Why does an agent's input bill grow so quickly over a long run?
options: Every iteration resends the accumulated context
The model reprocesses its full weights on every single step
Tool outputs are billed at a flat per-call fee
Caching multiplies the number of input tokens sent
questions.explanation: Each iteration resends the system prompt, history, and prior tool results, so the input side balloons as the loop continues, while the output side stays comparatively small.

questions.question: To make prompt caching effective, how should a prompt be ordered?
options: Variable content first, followed by the static content
Static content first, then the variable content
Newest message first, oldest message last
Longest sections first, shortest sections last
questions.explanation: Caching reuses an identical prefix, so keeping the static system prompt and tool definitions first and the variable user data last preserves cache hits.

questions.question: Why does context engineering tend to beat simply buying a larger context window?
options: Larger windows are billed at a flat rate regardless of use
Models ignore any content placed beyond the system prompt
Cost grows quadratically and recall drops as it fills
Larger windows cannot hold structured data
questions.explanation: Attention cost rises faster than the input, and models underuse information in the middle of long inputs, so curating fewer high-signal tokens beats stuffing the window.
